questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was evaluated for a new pleural effusion. He had recently returned from a 2-year residence in Honduras. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain and a nonproductive cough with a low-grade fever. His medical history was not remarkable. Investigations: CXR: moderate-sized left pleural effusion A thoracentesis was performed
questions.lead_in: What pleural fluid investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adenosine deaminase measurement The patient presents with a new pleural effusion after returning from an endemic area for tuberculosis. The concern is for a tuberculous effusion and an LDH, pH, or Gram stain would not help diagnose tuberculosis. An AFB stain would be low yield, and therefore the correct answer is an adenosine deaminase. An adenosine deaminase would be expected to be high in the setting of a tuberculous effusion, and of the choices listed would be the most helpful for establishing the diagnosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q12

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of fever, malaise, diarrhea, cough, and wheezing. He had returned 4 weeks earlier from a 3-week trip to Malawi. Prior to the trip he received HAV , typhoid, and Tdap vaccinations. He did not take malaria prophylaxis because he was concerned about possible side effects. During his trip he visited orphanages, participated in traditional baptism ceremonies in Lake Malawi, ate with locals, and visited a small hospital where he had contact with inpatients and outpatients. On examination his temperature was 38.2°C, and he had a widespread urticarial rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schistosomiasis Based on the incubation period and symptoms, the most likely diagnosis of the options provided is acute schistosomiasis. Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) is a hypersensitivity response to the start of egg production by the adult worms and manifests with a variety of symptoms, including fever, dry cough, diarrhea, urticaria, and angioedema. Measles, dengue, and Marburg (one of the hemorrhagic fevers) would not present this late. Malaria is not associated with a rash. (Image from James WD, Elston DM, McMahon PJ. Parasitic infestations, stings, and bites. In Andrews’ Diseases of the Skin Clinical Atlas. Elsevier; 2018.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q43

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and diarrhea. She had also noted recurrent but transient urticaria during this time. She had traveled with her family to Costa Rica 4 weeks earlier where she had eaten local food, which included raw shellfish. A diagnosis of paragonimiasis was confirmed by serology.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Praziquantel While both praziquantel and bithionol have activity against paragonimiasis, praziquantel is a better tolerated agent and therefore the more appropriate first-line therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q9

questions.question: A patient from the Caribbean presents with repeated gram-negative bacillary bacteremia.
questions.question_raw: Q26 (2013 PM). From Caribbean, repeat GNB bacteremia.

parts.text: Three steps in the pathogenesis of the causative organism?
What testing will confirm your diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: B) 3 steps in the pathogenesis of the causative organism?
C) What testing will confirm your diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: a) Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis. In a patient from a Strongyloides-endemic region (Caribbean), recurrent enteric gram-negative bacteremia is the classic clue: migrating filariform larvae carry gut flora into the bloodstream. b) (1) Filariform larvae penetrate skin (or perianal skin in autoinfection) and migrate via blood/lymphatics to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed. (2) In the small intestine they mature to adult females that produce eggs hatching into rhabditiform larvae. (3) Rhabditiform larvae transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut and reinvade the intestinal mucosa/perianal skin (autoinfection); under immunosuppression this cycle amplifies massively, disseminating larvae and translocating enteric GNB into the blood. c) Serial concentrated stool examination for larvae (plus sputum/duodenal aspirate in hyperinfection), and Strongyloides serology. d) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg daily; extend until stool and sputum are negative for ~2 weeks in hyperinfection/dissemination (add albendazole in disseminated disease), and reduce or reverse immunosuppression.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not covered in the Salmonella chapter; answer rests on standard ID knowledge and the Mandell Strongyloides chapter/IDSA guidance.

cohort_answer.text:
Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome
Filariform larvae in soil penetrate human skin and migrate to small intestine; Larvae migrate via bloodstream and lymphatics to lungs where they are eventually coughed and swallowed; In the small intestine, they become female adult worms that produce eggs in the intestinal mucosa that become rhabditiform larvae; Rhabditiform larvae in the gut become infective filariform larvae that can penetrate either the intestinal mucosa or the skin of the perianal area, resulting in autoinfection.
Concentrated stool examination for microscopy (larvae/eggs)
Hyperinfection: ivermectin x 7 days; Disseminated: Ivermectin + albendazole daily until stool/ sputum is neg x 2 weeks; Reduce immunosuppression

questions.model_answer: a) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (hyperresponsive immune reaction to Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi microfilariae; mimics refractory asthma). b) (1) Peripheral blood — marked eosinophilia and very high total IgE; (2) Serum — antifilarial antibody serology; (3) Tissue biopsy (lung/liver/lymph node) sampling for microfilariae/degenerating microfilariae (nocturnal blood smears are typically negative in TPE). c) (1) Diethylcarbamazine (DEC); (2) add-on doxycycline (anti-Wolbachia) or a macrocyclic lactone/albendazole; corticosteroids for the inflammatory response.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is a lymphatic filariasis syndrome (filarial nematode), not covered in this trematode chapter — answered from Mandell filariasis chapter and CDC guidance.

cohort_answer.text: A) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (response to Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi); causes dyspnea, cough, wheezing (esp night), chest discomfort, weight loss, malaise; commonly misdiagnosed as asthma; high eosinophils, high IgE, antifilarial antibodies; diffuse miliary lesions on CXR, patchy consolidation, cavitation, reticulonodular infiltrates, can lead to progressive fibrosis. Dx: microfilariae in lung/liver/lymph node bx. B) Nocturnal blood smear; anti-filarial antibodies; biopsy of lung/liver/lymph node for microfilaria; sputum for eosinophils; IgE and eosinophilia. C) DEC, Doxycycline, Ivermectin, Albendazole.

questions.question_raw: Would corticosteroids be indicated in the following conditions:

parts.text: Neurocysticercosis with viable parenchymal cysts and no evidence of intracranial hypertension
Hydatid cyst at high risk of rupture and spillage

parts_raw.text: Neurocysticercosis with viable parenchymal cysts and no evidence of intracranial hypertension
Hydatid cyst at high risk of rupture and spillage

questions.model_answer: a) Yes. Adjunctive corticosteroids with antituberculous therapy improve neurologic outcome and mortality in tuberculous meningitis and are recommended (they are also recommended for pericardial TB). b) Yes. When cysticidal therapy (albendazole ± praziquantel) is given for viable parenchymal cysts, corticosteroids are co-administered to blunt the peri-lesional inflammatory response provoked by dying cysts. c) Yes. Corticosteroids are used in acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) to control the systemic hypersensitivity reaction; praziquantel is added/repeated once acute illness settles. d) Yes. Peri-procedural corticosteroids are used around cyst manipulation (surgery or PAIR) to reduce the risk/consequences of anaphylaxis from spillage, alongside albendazole cover.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b–d are not covered in Mandell ch. 249; steroid use in neurocysticercosis, Katayama syndrome, and hydatid cyst manipulation reflects standard parasitology/IDSA-WHO practice.

questions.question: A woman returning from a beach vacation is shown to have lesions on her abdomen with multiple excoriations.
questions.question_raw: Q6 (2007). Woman returning from beach vacation. You are shown a poor quality picture of lesions on her abdomen, with multiple excoriations.
questions.model_answer: a) Cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption). b) Nematode — zoonotic hookworm larvae, Ancylostoma braziliense (also A. caninum). c) Clinical diagnosis from the serpiginous, migrating pruritic track and exposure history (dermoscopy supportive; stool microscopy not usually helpful as larvae do not mature in humans). d) Dog/cat feces deposit eggs in warm sand/soil; eggs hatch to rhabditiform then infective filariform larvae that penetrate human skin and migrate in the epidermis, unable to complete their cycle, producing the inflammatory track. e) Larva currens (Strongyloides stercoralis, faster-moving), gnathostomiasis, scabies, tinea, phytophotodermatitis. f) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO x1 (repeat if needed) or albendazole 400 mg PO daily x3-7 days.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by hookworm (nematode) larvae and is outside this trematode chapter — answered from Mandell hookworm/CLM material and CDC guidance.

cohort_answer.text: A) Cutaneous larva migrans. B) Ancylostoma Brasiliense/caninum. C) Clinical diagnosis based on history and appearance of rash; emerging dermoscopy reports; fecal microscopy if GI symptoms for hookworm eggs. D) Dogs/cats excrete eggs into soil; eggs hatch to release rhabditiform larva; rhabditiform larva mature into filariform larva after 5-10 days becoming infective; filariform larva in soil penetrate human skin and produce inflammatory reaction along cutaneous migration route. E) Strongyloides (causes 'Larva Currens', more rapid); Gnathostoma (larva causes local swelling - edema/pain/pruritis/erythema). F) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO x1-2 days.

parts.text: Give the three most common causes of asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient.
Give two reasons the stool ova and parasites is negative.

parts_raw.text: A) Give 3 most common causes for asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient
B) Give 2 reasons why the stool O+P is negative

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis. (2) Schistosoma species. (3) Hookworm (Necator americanus/Ancylostoma spp.). These soil-transmitted/tissue helminths are the most commonly identified parasites causing incidental eosinophilia in returning travellers/immigrants.
b) (1) Intermittent/low-level larval or egg excretion with low sensitivity of stool microscopy – Strongyloides sheds larvae intermittently, so up to ~7 stool examinations are needed to detect it. (2) It can take several weeks after infection for larvae/eggs to appear in stool (pre-patent period), and Schistosoma (S. haematobium) eggs may not be passed in stool at all; serology detects infection before/without stool positivity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Schistosoma is not covered in this chapter; its role as a common cause of eosinophilia and its stool-insensitivity (S. haematobium eggs in urine) are from the schistosomiasis chapter/CDC. The chapter supports Strongyloides and hookworm and the poor sensitivity/intermittent excretion of stool testing.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides, Schistosomiasis, and hookworm are most commonly identified parasites (network +REDIVI data: S. stercoralis 34.4%, Schistosoma sp 11.0%, hookworm 8.6%). Other infectious causes: Filariae, HIV-1, various helminths. Non-infectious: allergy/atopic disease, drug reaction, hypoadrenalism, tumor-associated, hypereosinophilic syndromes. B) Stool O+P is very insensitive for Strongyloides (intermittent shedding) and Schistosomiasis; parasite not always excreted in stool (S. haematobium eggs excreted in urine not stool); for strongyloides eggs degrade before leaving body, need to look for rhabditiform larvae specifically; interval from acquisition to positive test result can be 3-4 weeks before GI symptoms/worms in intestine.

questions.question: For each of the following, indicate whether you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): tuberculous meningitis; neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst; cerebral malaria; acute schistosomiasis; a large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR.
questions.question_raw: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario with rationale.

parts_raw.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

questions.model_answer: (1) TB meningitis: YES - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in confirmed TBM (not HIV+, where evidence is weaker). Note: steroids are NOT routine during purely empirical/diagnostic therapy as they blunt the clinical and CSF response and can worsen an undiagnosed fungal infection. (2) Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst: YES - corticosteroids control the peri-lesional inflammation/edema provoked by antiparasitic (albendazole) therapy; not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated edema. (3) Cerebral malaria: NO - randomized data show steroids are harmful (prolonged coma, more complications). (4) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama / acute neuroschistosomiasis): YES - corticosteroids given with praziquantel to suppress the hypersensitivity reaction. (5) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: NO - no role for adjunctive steroids; risk is anaphylaxis, managed with antihistamines/epinephrine and peri-procedural albendazole, not steroids.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the TB-meningitis point is touched in this chapter (p. 1225, advising against routine steroids during empirical therapy). Steroid use in confirmed TBM, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, and echinococcosis/PAIR rests on IDSA/WHO guidance and the respective Mandell disease chapters, not the chronic meningitis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

questions.model_answer: a) Schistosoma mansoni — a blood-fluke trematode of sub-Saharan Africa acquired through freshwater snail exposure; chronic infection causes periportal (Symmers 'pipestem') fibrosis, presinusoidal portal hypertension and splenomegaly. Treated with praziquantel.

cohort_answer.text: Schistosoma mansoni. Trematode (flat-worm) blood fluke. Typically found in sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, parts of North Africa (e.g. Egypt), Middle East. Infects humans from fresh water exposure where the snail intermediate host is present. Treatment: Praziquantel.

parts_raw.text: Identify the parasite: Patient from Zimbabwe with bladder fibrosis.

questions.model_answer: a) Schistosoma haematobium. A sub-Saharan African blood fluke whose adult worms reside in the vesical (bladder) venous plexus; chronic egg deposition in the bladder wall provokes granulomas, fibrosis, and ultimately calcification of the bladder wall, causing the genitourinary schistosomiasis seen here.

cohort_answer.text: Schistosoma haematobium. Trematode (flat-worm) blood fluke. Typically found in sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa, Middle East. Infects humans from fresh water exposure where the snail intermediate host is present. Treatment: Praziquantel.

questions.question: Which malignancies are associated with the following organisms?
questions.question_raw: Which malignancies are associated with the following organisms:
questions.model_answer:
a) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma (also non-Hodgkin lymphoma).
b) HPV - cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
c) Schistosoma haematobium - squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
d) Clonorchis sinensis - cholangiocarcinoma.
e) Helicobacter pylori - gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma.
f) HHV-8 - Kaposi sarcoma (also primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the HPV association is in this chapter; HCV, S. haematobium, Clonorchis, H. pylori and HHV-8 associations are established knowledge from other chapters/IARC.
